evidence.claim: Vermont Tourism presents the Stone Valley Byway as a journey through the region’s stone heritage, linking the Dorset Playhouse, Poultney’s historical museums and a Revolutionary War battlefield.
evidence.quote: Stone Valley Byway Many of Vermont’s southern communities are set in stone. The Stone Valley Byway celebrates that history, leading to acclaimed theater at the Dorset Playhouse, a Revolutionary War battlefield historic site and the museums operated by the Poultney Historical Society.

evidence.claim: In the Mettawee Valley, farmland opens out at the Pawlet Flats, where hay and corn grow; surrounding forests produce lumber and maple syrup.
evidence.quote: the Valley opens up in North Rupert as the "Pawlet Flats," rich farmland well-suited to hay, corn, and other crops. The surrounding forests produce lumber as well as maple syrup and related products.

evidence.claim: The road’s number has a history broader than this byway.
evidence.quote: The northern portion, from Poultney to Middlebury, was part of the New England road marking system's Route 30, from which VT 30 got its number.

evidence.claim: From 1922 to 1926, New England Route 30 ran from Granville, New York, through Poultney and north to Alburg.
evidence.quote: From 1922 until 1926, New England Route 30 (part of the New England road marking system) ran from Granville, New York, through Poultney (via New York State Route 22A), continuing north through Burlington, to Alburg.

evidence.claim: When northern sections became U.S. highways in 1926, Vermont subsequently extended the Route 30 designation southeast to Brattleboro.
evidence.quote: The northern sections of Route 30 were assigned in 1926 to U.S. Route 7 (US 7) from Middlebury to Burlington, and to US 2 from Burlington to Alburg. Soon afterwards, Vermont extended the Route 30 designation southeast to its current Brattleboro terminus.

evidence.claim: A later change left a mark at the former Jenks Tavern in East Rupert: its attached barn was demolished when Route 30 was realigned in 1948.
evidence.quote: It was also originally attached to a barn, which was demolished in 1948 when Route 30 was realigned.

evidence.claim: On July 7, 1777, British troops caught the American rear guard at Hubbardton during the retreat from Fort Ticonderoga.
evidence.quote: On the morning of July 7, 1777, British forces, under General Simon Fraser, caught up with the American rear guard of the forces retreating after the withdrawal from Fort Ticonderoga.

evidence.claim: Most of the American army had continued toward Castleton, while Seth Warner’s rear guard stopped to rest and gather stragglers.
evidence.quote: The bulk of General Arthur St. Clair's army retreated through Hubbardton to Castleton, while the rear guard, commanded by Seth Warner, stopped at Hubbardton to rest and pick up stragglers.

evidence.claim: German reinforcements helped scatter the Americans, but British losses ended pursuit of the main army.

evidence.claim: Their material began as ocean-floor clay, compressed into shale and transformed by heat and pressure as the Taconic Mountains rose.
evidence.quote: Millions of years ago, clays that accumulated on the ocean floor compressed into shale. When the ocean floor uplifted to form the Taconic Mountains, heat and pressure metamorphosed the shale into much harder slate.
